purpose: Capecitabine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer and colorectal (colon and rectal) cancer. It may be used alone or along with other cancer treatments. Your doctor prescribed it because it can help slow down or stop the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_it_works: Capecitabine is a pill that your body converts into a cancer-fighting drug called 5-fluorouracil once it gets inside you. This active drug works by interfering with cancer cells' ability to make the building blocks they need to grow and multiply. Because cancer cells are growing faster than normal cells, they are more affected by this process.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is hand-foot syndrome — redness, soreness, peeling, or blistering on your palms and the soles of your feet. You may also experience nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, mouth sores, tiredness, or stomach pain. Let your care team know right away if diarrhea becomes severe or if you develop sores in your mouth.
warnings: Call your doctor immediately if you have severe diarrhea (more than 4 times a day), severe nausea or vomiting, chest pain, signs of infection (fever over 100.4°F, chills), unusual bleeding or bruising, or signs of a blood clot. Do not take this medication if you are pregnant, as it can seriously harm an unborn baby. Avoid taking it with blood thinners like warfarin without close monitoring, as it can increase bleeding risk. Do not take it if you have severe kidney problems.
typical_dosing: Capecitabine is usually taken twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening — within 30 minutes after a meal (breakfast and dinner). It is commonly taken for 14 days in a row, followed by a 7-day break, making up a 21-day cycle. Your exact dose is calculated based on your body size and will be determined by your doctor. Always swallow the tablets whole with water.
